subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: There are three small ideas that build on each other. First, an algorithm is a set of steps in the right order — and the order matters. Second, we can follow the steps one after another, from start to finish. Third, an algorithm can be turned into code — the special language that tells a computer what to do — and a set of code that does a job is a program. So they become animators.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 1 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: These come straight from the textbook unit. By the end of the unit, the child should be able to:
Know what an algorithm is — a set of steps for a job, in the right order.
Follow the steps in an algorithm, one after another.
Know that an algorithm can be turned into code (a program the computer follows).
Join blocks in ScratchJr to make a character move.

concepts.title: Everyday steps (what is an algorithm?)
concepts.explanation:
We do jobs in steps. A set of steps for a job, done in the right order, has a special name: an algorithm. That is the only new word today.

Stand up and wash your hands in the air together, calling out each step: “First we turn on the tap. Then we get the soap. Then we scrub, scrub, scrub. Then we rinse. Then we dry.” Do it with big happy actions.
concepts.example: Those steps, in the right order, are called an algorithm. An algorithm is just steps for a job!
concepts.checkYourself: steps for a job. That is plenty for day one. Can you put two or three everyday steps into a sensible order?

concepts.title: Follow the steps, in order
concepts.explanation:
We follow the steps in an algorithm one after another, from first to last. The order matters. If we mix up the order, we get a muddle — even if all the steps are there.

Oh no! All the steps are here, but the order is silly. Order matters! Take 2 steps forward. Hop 1 time.
concepts.example: Clap 2 times. Then let a child be the leader.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you notice when the order is silly? Can you trace a simple path and say the moves (right, up, hop)? Can you follow a short list of steps in order?

concepts.title: Code and programs
concepts.explanation:
Computers follow steps too! The steps we give a computer are written in code. Code is the special language that tells a computer what to do. A set of code that does a job is called a program. We plan a program by first writing the algorithm — the steps — and then turning each step into a block of code.

One child is the robot (the computer). A robot can only do exactly what it is told — it cannot guess. Robot, take 2 steps forward. Now stop. Then give a fuzzy command like “go over there” and let the robot freeze and shrug.
concepts.example: “See? A computer only does the steps we give it — it cannot think for itself.”
concepts.checkYourself: Can you match a simple block to its job by its picture or colour? Can you put Start, Move, Stop in order?

concepts.title: Be an animator! Make it move in ScratchJr
concepts.explanation:
Now we become animators and make a character really move. We turn our algorithm into blocks, join them, and tap the green flag to run it. Our job: make a character move across and hop.

this is the one we will make move. our picture instructions. our GO button — we tap it to run the program. You can add a character by tapping the plus in the top-left corner — an animal, or a person, whatever they like. Open ScratchJr on a big tablet where everyone can see.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: be an animator! Make it move in ScratchJr. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tap the green flag to run it? Can you find a block by its colour and drag it to join the others?

concepts.title: Make it talk, and tap to start
concepts.explanation:
A character can do more than move — it can talk! We add the Say block (purple — it shows a speech bubble). We also meet a new start block, Start on Tap (yellow — the program runs when you tap the character, instead of the green flag).

Blue blocks move, purple blocks talk, yellow blocks start.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: make it talk, and tap to start. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you use the Say block with a short word? Can you know the difference between starting on the green flag and starting on a tap? Can you test your program and watch it work? Can you add a second character?

debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: All the steps are there, but the order is silly. Order is part of the algorithm. Point it out: put your shoes on, then your socks on top.

debugging.symptom: The computer knows what I mean.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: A computer cannot guess or think — it only does exactly what the blocks say. Use the Robot Game: give a fuzzy instruction and the robot freezes.

debugging.symptom: Blocks work even if they are not touching.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Blocks must click together in a row, like a jigsaw, or only the first one runs. Mixing up the yellow start blocks. If nothing happens, check which yellow block is on top. Show a gap, you can see nothing happens, then join them. Start on Green Flag runs when you tap the green flag at the top; Start on Tap runs when you tap the character itself.

debugging.symptom: A cartoon or a game just happens by magic.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Someone wrote the steps — the algorithm — to make it move. This is a lovely, empowering idea: people made it, so people like them can make one too.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

project.title: Unit 2 Project: Be an Animator
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be an Animator into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be an animator project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
